title: Indicators of Attack
summary: An indicator of attack describes the behaviour and intent of an adversary during an intrusion rather than a fixed artefact left behind. Where an indicator of compromise is a hash, domain, registry key or file path, an attack indicator is a pattern: an office document spawning a scripting interpreter, a service account authenticating to many hosts in a short window, a workstation resolving internal host names it has no reason to know, or one credential used from two distant countries within minutes. Because behaviour is far more expensive for an attacker to change than a tool name, attack indicators survive recompilation and infrastructure rotation and form the basis of behavioural detection and the later, harder-to-evade stages of intrusion analysis frameworks. They also link isolated events into one narrative across endpoints, identity and network telemetry. The mistake is treating a single behaviour as proof of intrusion, since backup jobs, administration scripts, vulnerability scanners and developer tooling produce nearly identical patterns. Behaviour needs a baseline, context and correlation before it justifies action.

beginner.definition: An indicator of attack is a sign that describes what an attacker is doing, not only what they left behind. A file name can be changed in a second, but the way an attacker breaks in changes slowly. So defenders watch behaviour, such as a strange login, a program starting another program, or data leaving at night. These signs help you find an intrusion that hides its tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers can rename a file or move to a new server address in minutes. If your detection only looks for those names and addresses, you lose them. Behaviour changes much more slowly, so it gives you a longer chance to notice. Behaviour also connects separate events into one story, such as a login, a new account and a large download. That story is what tells you an intrusion is really happening.
howItWorks: Sensors collect events from endpoints, servers, the network and the sign-in logs.
The events are joined so one activity can be followed across several systems.
Rules then look for behaviour that normal everyday work almost never produces.
Each alert carries context, like the user, the host and the time of day.
Analysts confirm or dismiss each alert and then feed that answer back.
Confirmed behaviour then becomes a new detection rule for the whole organisation.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman in a tall office building. He does not know every cleaner by name, so a list of names is not much use to him. Instead he watches behaviour, such as someone carrying a toolbox towards the server room at two in the morning. That person may change clothes or arrive in a different van, but the behaviour still gives them away. The watchman also checks the visitor book before he calls the police. Behaviour is the sign, and context decides the response.
takeaways: Watch what an attacker does, because behaviour is harder to change than a file name.
Behaviour needs context, so combine several events before you act on one.
Use confirmed attacks to write new detection rules that help everyone.

objectives: Explain what an indicator of attack is and how it differs from an indicator of compromise.
Describe how behavioural telemetry is collected, joined and correlated across sources.
Explain why attack indicators survive small changes in attacker tools and infrastructure.
Recognise legitimate activity that can resemble an attack and cause a false positive.
Turn a confirmed behaviour into a durable detection rule for the whole estate.
